data_section_full_text:
Our sample consists of class action lawsuits filed between 1996 and 2000. <sup>1</sup> We
search the Securities Class Action Clearinghouse website [(http://securities.stanford.](http://securities.stanford.edu/)
[edu/) for all class action lawsuits filed in this period under the Securities Act of 1934.](http://securities.stanford.edu/)
We also obtain the beginning and ending dates of each class period from this website.
The class period of our sample lawsuits averages 10 months.

For each of these sued firms, we calculate the earnings surprise as


<u>UE</u>

where unexpected earnings (UE) is defined as the earnings per share before
extraordinary items for the quarter in which the lawsuit ended, minus the analyst
consensus forecast from IBES. <sup>2</sup> We use the first available analyst consensus forecast
that is at least 2 weeks after the previous earnings announcement. The last closing
price (P) prior to these forecasts (also obtained from IBES) is used to scale the
unexpected earnings. This price must be at least $2 for the firm to be included in the
sample. Because we are interested in examining the disclosure choices of firms facing
bad news, we select those lawsuits in which UE/P is less than or equal to �1%.

To ensure that all of the lawsuits in our sample relate to both earnings and
disclosure, we read through the complaints. This process leads us to omit several
types of cases. Specifically, we first omit those firms whose lawsuits do not relate to
current earnings. For example, a case in which the firm was sued for misleading
investors as to the status of a drug in the FDA approval process would not be
included in our sample. In this case, the lawsuit does not relate to current earnings
because the drug was not yet in production or being sold.

Second, we omit lawsuits that pertain entirely to an accounting irregularity as
opposed to a disclosure-related matter. <sup>3</sup> Early disclosure is not a viable means of
deterring accounting-irregularity lawsuits, and thus we would not expect a relation
between disclosure and the risk of being named in such a suit. Specifically, a case in
which a firm was sued for a GAAP violation would be considered an accountingirregularity lawsuit and excluded from our sample. However, a case in which a firm
was sued for concealing information about a loss of a major contract would be
considered a disclosure-related lawsuit, and it would be included in our sample. The
distinction between these two types of lawsuits is especially important given that our
sample period follows the enactment of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act
of 1995. Grundfest and Perino (1997) find that this Act resulted in a shift

2We have also conducted the analysis using a seasonal change in EPS as the measure of earnings
disappointment, as in Skinner (1997), where unexpected earnings is measured as reported earnings for the
current quarter less reported earnings for the same fiscal quarter of the previous year. Using this more
naı ̈ve measure of unexpected earnings, we find qualitatively similar results to those reported in this paper.

3We have also rerun all our tests including both accounting-related and disclosure-related lawsuits, and
we obtain qualitatively similar results.

The sample consists of 78 securities lawsuits in 1996–2000. Firms must have had an earnings surprise of at
least �1% in the quarter in which the lawsuit ended, and the lawsuit must specifically pertain to the
disclosure of an earnings-related matter. We obtain the sample by reading the complaints of class action
lawsuits filed between 1996 and 2000 under the Securities Acts of 1933 and 1934, as listed on the Securities
Class Action Clearinghouse website [(http://securities.stanford.edu/).](http://securities.stanford.edu/)


toward accounting-related lawsuits, as disclosure-related lawsuits became harder
to pursue.

Finally, we require firms to be covered by the CRSP, Compustat, and IBES
databases. Table 1 shows the distribution of lawsuits across years. We find between
14 and 19 lawsuits in each year, with no noticeable trend over the period.
To form a control sample, we obtain an equal number of non-sued firms. For each
sued firm, we randomly select a non-sued firm from the same quarter with CRSP,
Compustat, and IBES data, with a price of at least $2, and with an earnings
disappointment of at least –1% (defined in the same manner). After imposing these
screens, the data set consists of 78 sued firms and 78 non-sued firms. <sup>4</sup>

For both the sued and the non-sued firms, we search Factiva to determine whether
or not they disclosed the bad news prior to the earnings announcement. Specifically,
we search the major news and business publications, the top 50 newspapers, and the
press release wires. For each firm, the potential disclosure window spans
approximately one quarter. The last day of this window is one day before the
earnings announcement in the surprise quarter, and the first day is 7 days after the
prior quarterly earnings announcement. By definition, this window extends
substantially beyond the end of the fiscal quarter (since the scheduled earnings
announcement typically occurs weeks after the quarter end). It is thus reasonable to
assume that firms have some knowledge of the impending earnings disappointments
during this window, and they have the choice of whether or not to disclose the
information early.

4Since the population of sued firms with negative earnings surprises is smaller than the set of non-sued
firms with negative earnings surprises, we over-sample the sued firms. The advantage of the matched
sample methodology is its cost effectiveness in data collection. While we have collected data on all the sued
firms, it would be infeasible to collect similar disclosure data on the population of non-sued firms.
Unfortunately, the matched sample methodology has some potential limitations, which we discuss later.

ARTICLE IN PRESS

492 L. Field et al. / Journal of Accounting and Economics 39 (2005) 487–507


We search for firm disclosures related to earnings, such as announcements
regarding the magnitude of upcoming earnings, announcements that sales or
revenues will be lower than expected or costs will be higher than expected, and
announcements about write-offs or incurring restructuring charges. Of the 156 firms
in our sample, we find that 108 choose to disclose early, while 48 do not. Since we
examine the effects of early disclosure on the probability of being sued, we do not
include disclosures made by firms after the lawsuit is filed.

As discussed above, one of the primary ways that disclosure decreases the
probability of being sued is by decreasing the amount of time that the stock trades at
the allegedly misleading price, thereby decreasing potential recoverable damages.
This effect is obviously greater for a firm that discloses long before the scheduled
earnings announcement date, compared to a firm that discloses the bad news just a
few days ahead of time. There are two firms in the sample that disclose less than 5
days prior to the scheduled earnings announcement. These disclosures do not
materially affect the period over which potential damages are measured, meaning
they are unlikely to dissuade a lawsuit. To increase the statistical power of our tests,
we eliminate these two firms and their respective match firms (although the results
are robust to including these observations). <sup>5</sup> This yields a final data set of 76 sued
firms and 76 non-sued firms.
